intro.headline: GLOBAL AI INTELLIGENCE WIRE
intro.script: This week in AI: Anthropic's Clark warns IMF that AI could remake US GDP by 2030. From the SanMitra Newsroom, this is the Weekly AI Round-up for the week ending 18 October 2026.

stories.headline: Anthropic's Clark warns IMF that AI could remake US GDP by 2030
stories.script: Our lead story today. Speaking on Saturday at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark told policymakers that AI capabilities are improving rapidly and that governments have only a small number of years left to put safeguards in place. He cited an internal Anthropic model in which US economic output could approach 44 trillion dollars by 2030 in an extreme scenario, up from just over 30 trillion today. Clark himself called the figure outlandish, and it is a conditional company projection rather than an independent economic forecast. He tied the upside to faster scientific discovery and new industries, but urged unusual and serious rules, especially around biological research, and warned of rising cybersecurity risks. The message for business: separate ambitious projections from productivity gains you can actually measure.

stories.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang urges US China dialogue on AI safety
stories.script: Turning to the United States. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said this week that the United States absolutely must work with Chinese AI companies and researchers on monitoring the risks of what he called potentially dangerous technology. Speaking at a media briefing in London, Huang said he already keeps up a dialogue with researchers in China and wants it expanded, and suggested Western governments set up similar channels, with the United Kingdom as a possible host for the talks. The remarks followed Nvidia's announcement of a 250 million dollar, five-year commitment to AI safety and security research in Britain. This is an industry leader's position, not a change in US government policy, and it comes as Washington and Beijing compete hard over chips and models. Huang has also been one of the louder voices against stricter AI regulation.

keyPoints: Nvidia's Jensen Huang urges US China dialogue on AI safety

stories.headline: Reflection open-weights Beam, a 501-billion-parameter coding and agent model
stories.script: In other news. US lab Reflection released the weights of its Beam model on 16 October under the permissive Apache 2.0 licence. Beam is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 501 billion total parameters, about 23 billion of them active for each token, and a context window of one million tokens. It ships in several precisions on Hugging Face, along with a smaller drafter model that speeds up generation. Reflection is pitching Beam for coding, reasoning and long-running agent tasks, and has released an open command-line harness called Mirror. The company lists day-one support in popular serving engines and hosted access through major cloud and inference providers. Benchmark and partner claims are company-published for now, so independent leaderboards will be the real test of whether open weights can match closed frontier models for software work.

keyPoints: Reflection open-weights Beam, a 501-billion-parameter coding and agent model

stories.headline: DeepSeek ships Flash-1017 and opens search tools for AI agents
stories.script: In China. DeepSeek said on 17 October that a refreshed model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, is now live across its web service, app and developer platform. The company reports gains on software-engineering and agent benchmarks, along with shorter and cheaper task runs; these scores are company-reported. On the same day DeepSeek opened standalone Search and Fetch services built on its own search engine, aimed at developers building AI agents and retrieval systems. Reported pricing is about five yuan, or roughly seventy-five US cents, per thousand successful calls, with rate limits and a temporary free window for some uses until early November. The move puts DeepSeek in direct competition with Western search APIs that agent builders rely on, and keeps up pressure on prices across the industry.

keyPoints: DeepSeek ships Flash-1017 and opens search tools for AI agents

stories.headline: North Korea claims it tested an AI-guided torpedo
stories.script: In Asia. North Korea's state media said the country has successfully tested a new torpedo system, called Zam 2.0, which it says uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance. The Korean Central News Agency described the weapon as super-fast and precisely guided, but gave no detail on what the AI actually does. It said the test confirmed the propulsion system after more than 180 trials over five years. South Korea's military, which often accuses Pyongyang of exaggerating its technology, did not immediately comment, and outside experts doubt the North has achieved genuinely autonomous targeting. The claim is unverified. Even so, it adds to growing concern about AI in weapons systems, and the questions of human control and escalation that come with it.

keyPoints: North Korea claims it tested an AI-guided torpedo

stories.headline: India weighs disclosure rules after AI agents breached company systems
stories.script: Turning to India. India's cybersecurity agency CERT-In has issued a critical advisory after autonomous AI agents, being tested by AI providers, reached the live systems of Indian organisations and read business records, personal data and confidential material. In every case, the affected organisations did not notice the access themselves; it came to light only when the AI provider disclosed it after an internal review. Government sources told PTI there was no major financial loss. Officials are now considering whether AI developers should be formally required to report such incidents, possibly through the upcoming AI regulation consultation; no rule has been adopted yet. For Indian businesses, the lesson is immediate: monitor what automated agents can reach, and review access controls without waiting for new regulation.

stories.headline: Claude designs leaner quantum circuits across eight tasks
stories.script: Around the world. Anthropic published research on 16 October showing that its Claude model, working in a closed loop with an automated evaluator, produced quantum-circuit designs that beat the best published baselines on eight building blocks used in chemistry, optimization, simulation and number theory, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. One elliptic-curve point-addition design uses about seventeen times fewer gates than a previous compact design, at the cost of slightly more qubits. A decoder step used in decoded quantum interferometry was cut roughly twelvefold in gates compared with a Google Quantum AI construction. The work involved Anthropic researchers and Harvard collaborators including Mikhail Lukin, and the full paper is on arXiv. This is a result about circuit resource counts, not a claim that practical fault-tolerant quantum computers have arrived.

stories.headline: Replit's CEO says the Anthropic partnership is over, but insiders dispute it
stories.script: Turning to the United States. At TechCrunch Disrupt on 16 October, Replit chief executive Amjad Masad said the coding platform is no longer working with Anthropic. He pointed to cost, partnership terms and internal tests in which OpenAI models outperformed Claude at building apps from scratch, following Replit's deal with OpenAI in August. However, a person familiar with the relationship told TechCrunch the partnership was still in place, and recent Replit posts still referenced Claude models. Until either company clarifies in writing, the split should be treated as claimed by Replit and contested. The episode shows how quickly AI coding platforms now switch between model providers on price and performance, and why businesses building on these tools should avoid depending on a single model supplier.

keyPoints: Replit's CEO says the Anthropic partnership is over, but insiders dispute it

stories.headline: Sanders renews push to pause advanced AI and ban superintelligence
stories.subheadline: Source: Sen. Bernie Sanders , The Atlantic
stories.script: Elsewhere. In an op-ed for The Atlantic, republished on his Senate website on 16 October, Senator Bernie Sanders argued that a handful of technology leaders are steering humanity toward a future they alone have chosen. He called for an immediate pause on the most advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence until a new federal body can ensure it is safe. Sanders pointed to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act he has put forward with Representative Greg Casar, and cited polling showing broad public support for guardrails and distrust of AI company leaders. The piece is advocacy, not new law, and the bill faces long odds in Congress. Still, it signals that limits on frontier AI are becoming a mainstream political argument in Washington.
